del_family: X resistor of # Ω has # X across it. What current flows?
# X is across a # kΩ resistor. Current?
X resistor has # X across it with # X flowing through it. It
X # Ω resistor carries # X. The power dissipated is:

new.q: What unit is mAh a measure of?
new.w: mAh = current × time, which is charge, not energy.

new.q: One joule per coulomb is the definition of which unit?
new.w: Voltage is energy per charge: 1 V = 1 J/C.
sol: 1 A = 1 C/s and 1 W = 1 J/s are the other two.

new.q: Convert 250 mA to amperes.
sol: Trap: moving the decimal the wrong way.

new.q: A 12 V battery moves 5.0 C of charge through a circuit. How much energy does it deliver, in joules?
To measure the current through a bulb, an ammeter must be placed:
o: next to the bulb, not in the circuit
new.w: Current must flow through the meter, so it goes in the path.
sol: Trap: parallel ammeter shorts the part.

new.q: A voltmeter measures the voltage across a resistor. It is connected:
new.w: Voltage is a difference between two points, so the meter bridges them.
sol: Voltage is measured across a part.

new.q: Write the resistor color bands (first three colors) for 10 Ω: digit 1, digit 0, multiplier ×1.
new.w: Brown = 1, black = 0 and black multiplier = ×1 → 10 Ω.

new.q: Three bands red, red, red (then gold). Give the value in kΩ as a number.
A 220 Ω resistor has ±10% tolerance. Which value could it measure?
new.w: 10% of 220 is 22, so range is 198 to 242 Ω.

new.q: A 100 Ω resistor is tested on a meter and reads 108 Ω. Its tolerance band must be at least:
new.w: 108 is 8% above 100, so 5% fails and 10% passes.
sol: Gold 5% is too tight, silver 10% works.

new.q: Select ALL that equal one joule.
new.w: J = W·s = V·C, and A·V·s is the same as W·s. W/s is not energy.

new.q: Match each quantity to its formula.
A 1500 W kettle is used for 90 minutes in total over a day. Energy used in kWh?
new.w: E = P·t with kW and hours.

new.q: A 100 W computer runs nonstop for 30 days. Electricity is $0.25 per kWh. Total cost in dollars?
A 2000 mAh battery is rated 3.7 V. How much charge is that in coulombs?
sol: Voltage is not needed for charge.

new.q: A 3.7 V, 2000 mAh battery powers a motor that draws a steady 0.50 A. How long does it last, in hours (ideal case)?
A 12 V car battery stores 50 Ah. How much energy is that, in Wh?
The 600 Wh car battery powers a 60 W lamp. How many hours (ideal case)?
An EV needs 40 kWh. The charger delivers 7.0 kW. How many hours to charge (ideal)? Give one decimal.
A wire carries 20 A and has resistance 0.050 Ω. How many watts are wasted as heat in the wire?
sol: Trap: P = V·I with the full supply voltage.

new.q: A 9.0 V supply lights an LED that needs 2.0 V and 20 mA. Resistor needed to limit current, in ohms?
new.w: The resistor takes the leftover voltage.

new.q: A 100 W and a 60 W bulb (both 120 V) are wired in series across 120 V. Which glows brighter?
new.w: Series current is equal; the 60 W bulb has more resistance so P = I²R is larger.
sol: P = I²R is bigger for 240 Ω.

new.q: A 120 V, 60 W bulb is run on 60 V. Treating its resistance as constant, what power does it use?
The voltage across a fixed resistor is halved. The power becomes:
sol: Trap: P is not proportional to V.

new.q: A heater's supply voltage stays fixed. Its resistance is cut to half. The heat produced per second:
new.w: P = V²/R, so lower R means more power.
sol: Trap: thinking more resistance means more heat at fixed voltage.

new.q: Both the voltage across a resistor and the resistance are halved. The power becomes:
sol: Dividing by half R doubles it: ¼ × 2 = ½.

new.q: A wire is stretched uniformly to twice its length (same total volume of metal). Its resistance becomes:
new.w: Longer AND thinner both raise R.

new.q: A 2.0 Ω wire is stretched uniformly to three times its length (volume unchanged). New resistance in ohms?
new.w: R ∝ L² when volume is fixed.

new.q: A wire has twice the diameter and twice the length of another wire of the same metal. Its resistance compared with the other is:
new.w: Length ×2 → R ×2. Diameter ×2 → R ÷4. Net ½.
sol: Trap: forgetting area depends on diameter².

new.q: A 12 Ω wire is cut into four equal pieces. The pieces are twisted together side by side to make one thick wire. What is its resistance in ohms?
sol: Four 3 Ω paths side by side: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 Ω.

new.q: A wire has resistance 8.0 Ω. Another wire of the same metal has half the length and half the diameter. Its resistance in ohms?
new.w: Half length gives ½; half diameter gives ×4.

new.q: How many times larger is the resistance of an aluminum wire than a copper wire of the same length and area? (ρ Al 2.65, Cu 1.68, ×10⁻⁸ Ω·m) One decimal place.
A copper wire (ρ = 1.68×10⁻⁸ Ω·m) is 2.0 m long with area 0.50 mm². Its resistance in ohms?
new.w: R = ρL/A with area in m².

new.q: A copper wire has resistance 10.0 Ω at 20 °C. Resistance rises 0.39% per °C (R = R₀(1 + 0.0039·ΔT)). Resistance at 70 °C, in ohms?
A tungsten bulb filament is cold. At the instant it is switched on, compared with normal glow, the current is:
new.w: Hot metal has more resistance, so cold filament resistance is low.
sol: I = V/R is large at first.
Current then falls as it warms.

new.q: A bulb draws 0.50 A at 120 V when glowing. Its cold resistance is 20 Ω. What is the switch-on current in amperes?
Current enters a bulb at 2.0 A. The current leaving the bulb is:
o: less than 2.0 A, since the bulb uses it
new.w: Charge is not used up; energy is.
sol: The bulb converts energy, not current.

new.q: A power line carries 1.0 MW at 10 kV through wires of total resistance 2.0 Ω. Power lost in the wires, in kW? (I = P/V)
The same line now sends 1.0 MW at 100 kV (10 times higher voltage), same 2.0 Ω wires. Power lost, in kW?
Two 100 Ω, ¼ W resistors are in series. What is the largest supply voltage that keeps both within their rating, in volts?
new.w: Same current; each limited to 50 mA.

new.q: Two 100 Ω, ¼ W resistors are in parallel. Largest supply voltage within ratings, in volts?
new.w: Same voltage; each limited by V = √(PR).
sol: Each resistor carries 50 mA at that point.

new.q: A 1.0 kΩ, ¼ W resistor. What is the largest voltage across it, in volts? One decimal.
A 15 A breaker protects a 120 V circuit. What is the largest total power it allows, in watts?
sol: A 1500 W heater plus 800 W toaster draws 19 A and trips it.

new.q: A 120 V, 15 A circuit runs a 1500 W heater and an 800 W toaster. What happens?
o: The breaker trips; the total is 19 A
It runs; each appliance has its own 15 A
It runs; current adds only in series
new.w: Appliances share the circuit, so their currents add.
sol: Trap: thinking each device has a separate limit.

new.q: A kettle heats 1.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. Water: 4186 J/(kg·°C). How many joules?
A 1500 W kettle is 80% efficient and heats 1.0 kg of water by 80 °C (4186 J/(kg·°C)). Time needed in seconds?
A motor is 80% efficient and drives a gearbox that is 90% efficient. Overall efficiency, as a percent?
An LED driver takes in 5.0 W and gives out 3.5 W of light, wasting 1.5 W as heat. Efficiency in percent?
A 1.5 A current flows for 2.0 minutes. About how many electrons pass a point? (e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C) Answer in scientific notation, e.g. 1.1e21.
A 1.0 A current is how many electrons per second? (e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C), e.g. 6.2e18.
Table: V = 2, 4, 6 V gives I = 0.10, 0.18, 0.24 A. What does it show?
o: Resistance rises with voltage, so not ohmic
Resistance falls with voltage, so not ohmic
new.w: V ÷ I = 20, 22, 25 Ω. An ohmic part has constant R.
sol: Trap: using only the first row.

new.q: Order these same-length wires by resistance, lowest first.
Order by energy, smallest first.
Select ALL changes that raise a wire's resistance.
new.w: R = ρL/A, and hotter metal has more R. Gold ρ (2.44) is above copper (1.68).

new.q: A 30 m copper cable (1.5 mm²) feeds a load, so current travels 60 m in total out and back. It carries 10 A. Voltage lost in the cable, in volts? (ρ = 1.68×10⁻⁸ Ω·m)
new.w: Find R of the full loop, then V = IR.

new.q: A 10 Ω and a 40 Ω resistor are in series across 20 V. Power in the 40 Ω resistor, in watts?
sol: Trap: using the full 20 V across it.

new.q: A 10 Ω and a 40 Ω resistor are each connected alone across the same 20 V. Which dissipates more power?
o: 40 Ω: higher R means more heat
new.w: With fixed voltage, P = V²/R, so smaller R gives more power.
sol: Opposite rule holds with fixed current.

new.q: A converter that is 85% efficient runs a 2.5 W device from a 9.25 Wh battery. Battery input power is 2.5 ÷ 0.85. Run time in hours?
new.w: Battery supplies more than the device uses.

new.q: A 5.0 V charger outputs 2.0 A and is 85% efficient. Input power from the wall, in watts? One decimal.
A 24 Ω heater carries 0.50 A for 10 minutes. Energy in joules?
new.w: P = I²R, then E = Pt with t in seconds.

new.q: The kilowatt-hour on your electric bill is a unit of:
Current through a fixed resistor doubles. Compared with before, the heat per second is:
sol: Trap: thinking P doubles with I.

report: Found numeric-key errors (wrong units/scale): 007 (0.05 mA should be 50 mA), 028 (0.02 mA -> 20 mA), 031 (1080000 kWh -> 0.30), 033 (302400 Wh -> 84), 034 (5544 h -> 1.54), 128-130 (family of kΩ current: key in A but unit mA; family likely wrong, deleted via del_family header text, ids 128-130 fixed anyway), 023 (tol 0.5 pct too tight for 5.556). Re-leveled 007,008,015,016 from 3 to 2. Deleted ~100 near-identical resistor color-code items (kept 6 plus 017/018) and 3 duplicate trivial families (043 I=V/R, 263 R=V/I, 342 P=I2R; del ids + del_family by header text since fp keys not visible). Added 62 questions, about half level 3: wire stretching/folding, series/parallel power ratings, transmission loss, cold filament, breaker, efficiency chains, resistivity, temperature coefficient. Doubts: del_family keys are header strings, caller should resolve to fp; cold-resistance q assumes metal filament; study note says '1/4 W 100 ohm' which is fine.
